analysis.one_liner: Removes the federal exemption that lets freight companies deny truck drivers overtime pay.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or vote, despite a bipartisan Republican-Democratic sponsor team.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal overtime law has a carve-out: workers employed by motor carriers — most long-haul and regional truck drivers — can be required to work 60 or 70 hours a week with no overtime pay, even past 40 hours. This bill strikes that carve-out from the Fair Labor Standards Act, so freight and motor carrier employers would owe drivers time-and-a-half beyond 40 hours like most other hourly workers. It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Truck drivers employed by motor carriers — the group currently excluded from overtime — who would earn time-and-a-half pay for hours beyond 40 in a week. Long-haul drivers who routinely work 60-70 hour weeks under the freight industry's per-mile pay structure would see the largest gains.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes Section 13(b)(1) of the Fair Labor Standards Act, the provision that exempts motor carrier employees from federal overtime requirements.
Brings motor carrier employees under the same overtime rules as most other hourly workers, so hours beyond 40 in a week would have to be paid at time-and-a-half.
Was introduced by a Republican (Rep. Van Drew) with a Democratic co-lead (Rep. Takano), giving it at least nominal bipartisan support from the start.

analysis.who_pays: Motor carriers, trucking companies, and freight shippers, who would face higher payroll costs for long workweeks. Some of that cost would likely pass through to shipping customers and consumers as higher freight rates.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on motor carriers and would likely be passed to shippers and consumers through higher freight rates, at least in part.

Many drivers are paid per mile rather than by the hour; converting to overtime-eligible hourly pay would require the industry to restructure compensation, and opponents could argue some drivers prefer mileage-based pay tied to productivity.
Federal hours-of-service rules already cap truckers' driving hours, so the bill raises pay for long weeks rather than shortening them; it does not by itself reduce fatigue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a direct wage gain for a large, overworked occupational group that is uniquely excluded from a near-universal pay protection, and the cost is higher freight payroll that the industry can price into rates. The main weakness is design: because many drivers are paid by the mile, the bill would need implementing rules to translate overtime into that pay structure, and it does not address the fatigue drivers face — it only makes long weeks more expensive for employers. On balance it is a straightforward, narrow pay fix for an excluded workforce.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no markup, no vote — so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Van Drew introduced the bill on November 9, 2023, joined by Rep. Takano as co-lead, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The bill's only action was that referral; the full action history shows nothing further, meaning no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action ever occurred.
It attracted 3 cosponsors (2 Democrats, 1 Republican) and sat until the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Motor carriers and freight shippers are better off: they avoided a change that would have required overtime pay for drivers working long weeks, and no record shows any effort to move the bill forward. Drivers remain excluded from overtime.

for.name: Rep. Jefferson Van Drew
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; recruited a Democratic co-lead.

for.name: Rep. Mark Takano
for.what_they_did: Joined Van Drew in introducing the bill on the day it was filed.

for.name: Cosponsors (2 Democrats, 1 Republican)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; the bill never grew beyond this small bipartisan group.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Rep. Virginia Foxx (R-NC)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after referral, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Trucking and freight industry
against.role: Motor carriers that benefit from the overtime exemption
against.what_they_did: The industry has long relied on the motor carrier exemption that keeps most truck drivers out of federal overtime; no organized defense was needed because the bill never moved.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican with a Democratic co-lead, and its three cosponsors split 2 Democrats and 1 Republican; no opposition ever appeared on the record, so the partisan shape is undefined.

industries.note: The bill would end their exemption from federal overtime law, requiring time-and-a-half pay after 40 hours for drivers they currently schedule for 60-70 hour weeks at per-mile rates. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against drivers' paychecks.
Higher trucking payroll would likely raise freight rates somewhat, but shippers also depend on driver retention, and better pay could reduce the chronic driver turnover that disrupts deliveries.
